references: ASTM D5430 - Standard Test Methods for Visually Inspecting and Grading Fabrics (4-point system)
ASTM D3882 - Standard Test Method for Bow and Skew in Woven and Knitted Fabrics
ISO 13015 - Textiles: determination of distortion (bow and skew) in woven fabrics
ISO 105-A02 - Grey scale for assessing change in colour

hole_tear.name: Hole / Tear / Cut
hole_tear.description: An opening in the fabric where yarns are broken or missing in both directions.

causes.cause: Damaged or burred reed dents, temples (temple rings/rollers) or shuttle/rapier/gripper cutting yarns
Excessive warp tension or beat-up force combined with weak yarn
Chemical damage: concentrated acid, alkali, bleach or reducing agent spots weaken fibres, which later break into holes
Mechanical damage from stenter pins/clips, rough guide rollers, or fabric caught in machinery
Damage during transport, unpacking (knife cuts), hooks, forklift tines, or insects/rodents in storage

remedy: Mark the defect and cut it out during inspection (cut-and-mark / fents), or downgrade the piece
Small holes in high-value fabric: mend by darning (invisible mending) before finishing
Find the source: check for a repeating hole position (same distance apart = rotating machine part)
prevention: Regular inspection and polishing/replacement of reeds, temples and insertion elements
Control chemical concentration and avoid undissolved chemical spots; rinse thoroughly
Maintain rollers, guides and stenter pins; safe packing and handling procedures

stain.name: Stain / Spot (oil, dirt, rust, dye)
stain.description: A localized discoloured area caused by foreign matter such as oil, grease, dirt, rust or dye.

causes.cause: Oil or grease from over-lubricated loom parts dripping or splashing onto the fabric
Dirty hands, dirty fly/fluff mixed with oil, dirty cloth rollers or trolleys
Undissolved dyestuff or chemical particles, water/condensate drops before drying, dye spots
Rust from wet fabric contacting iron surfaces
Ink/marker, dust and soil during storage and transport; uncovered fabric rolls

remedy: Identify the stain type first (oil, rust, dye, dirt) - the treatment depends on it
Oil/grease: spot-clean with a suitable solvent or detergent (stain-removal gun), then rewash
Rust: treat with an oxalic-acid based rust remover, then rinse
If the stain remains: re-scour/rewash the batch, or cut out / downgrade
prevention: Correct lubrication amount, drip guards and regular cleaning of looms
Clean trolleys and rollers, covered fabric rolls, clean hands/gloves
Filter and fully dissolve dyes and chemicals; avoid condensate dripping in steamers/dryers
Use stainless steel or coated surfaces where wet fabric touches metal

slub_neps.name: Slub / Neps (thick places in yarn)
slub_neps.description: Slub: a short, abnormally thick place in a yarn. Neps: small tangled knots of fibres on the yarn/fabric surface.

causes.cause: Faulty drafting: roller lapping, eccentric or worn drafting rollers, wrong roller settings (slubs)
Fly and fluff caught and spun into the yarn, bad piecing (slubs)
Poor carding: worn card clothing or wrong card settings, excessive beating in opening (neps)
Immature / dead cotton fibres that tangle easily (neps; often appear as white specks after dyeing)
Accumulated fly/fluff on the loom falling into the shed and being woven in

remedy: Grey fabric: remove prominent slubs/neps by burling (careful pulling/trimming) during mending
Neps that stay white after dyeing: consider topping/re-dyeing with dyes that cover immature cotton better
Repeated slubs: trace the yarn lot and inform the spinning department/supplier; reject the yarn lot if needed
prevention: Specify yarn quality (Uster IPI thick places and neps per km, Classimat faults)
Electronic yarn clearers at winding to cut out thick places
Card maintenance (clothing, settings) and good fibre selection (maturity)
Regular cleaning of looms (blowing/suction) to remove fly

broken_pick_end.name: Broken / Missing End or Pick
broken_pick_end.description: Broken end: a warp yarn is missing or broken (lengthwise line). Broken/missing pick: a weft yarn is missing or broken (crosswise line).

causes.cause: Poor sizing (low size add-on, uneven sizing) so warp yarns break from abrasion during weaving
Weak or uneven yarn (low strength, thin places)
Excessive or uneven warp tension; rough or damaged healds, drop wires or reed
Warp stop motion not working, so the loom keeps running after an end breaks
Weft insertion failure: weft breakage, wrong weft tension/feeder, nozzle timing (air-jet), weft stop motion failure
Incorrect pick finding/restart after a stop (also causes start-up marks)

remedy: Grey fabric: mend by drawing in the missing end/pick by hand (mending)
Long continuous broken end along the piece: cut out or downgrade the piece
Repair the loom immediately: check and reset warp and weft stop motions
prevention: Optimise sizing recipe and size add-on; good warp preparation
Correct and uniform warp tension; maintain healds, drop wires and reeds
Regular checks of warp/weft stop motions and weft insertion settings
Yarn strength specification; operator training on correct pick finding

shade_variation.name: Shade Variation
shade_variation.description: Colour difference within a piece (side-centre-side 'listing', end-to-end) or between pieces/lots.

causes.cause: Batch-to-batch (dye lot) differences: recipe, weighing or water quality variation
Uneven dye liquor circulation, temperature or pH variation in the machine (jet, jigger, beam)
Uneven padding pressure across the width (side-centre-side shading / listing)
Uneven scouring/bleaching/mercerising, giving uneven absorbency
Uneven drying or heat-setting temperature across the stenter width
Mixing fibre lots with different dye affinity (e.g. maturity, polyester merge number)

remedy: Shade sorting: group pieces into shade bands so each garment uses one shade (continuity cards)
Shade correction: topping/re-dyeing to match the standard, or stripping and re-dyeing
Listing: re-pad after calibrating padder pressure across the width
prevention: Lab-to-bulk recipe control and spectrophotometer checks against the approved standard
Stable process parameters: temperature, pH, liquor ratio, time
Uniform pretreatment; regular padder roller pressure calibration
Control fibre/yarn lots (do not mix lots in one order)

bowing.name: Bowing (bow)
bowing.description: Weft yarns are curved (arc shape) across the fabric width instead of straight.

causes.cause: Fabric centre travelling slower or faster than the selvedges (centre lagging) on stenter or rollers
Uneven tension or overfeed across the width; worn or bent rollers
No or badly adjusted weft straightener (bow rollers) before the stenter

remedy: Re-run the fabric through a weft straightener (bow rollers) before setting, then re-set on the stenter
Heat-set synthetic fabrics are difficult to correct after setting - correct before heat-setting
prevention: Automatic weft straightener with optical weft sensors at stenter entry
Check roller alignment and uniform tension across width

skewing.name: Skewing (skew)
skewing.description: Weft yarns are straight but slanted - not perpendicular to the selvedges.

causes.cause: Unequal feeding of the two selvedges on the stenter (one side over-fed)
Misaligned rollers or uneven batching/winding tension
No or badly adjusted weft straightener (skew rollers)
Twill weave torque or uneven take-up can contribute to skew

remedy: Re-run through weft straightener (skew rollers) and re-stenter with equal selvedge feeding
Correct before heat-setting for synthetic fabrics
prevention: Weft straightener with automatic control; equal overfeed on both sides of the stenter
Regular roller alignment checks
